steps.title: Whole berries
steps.body: In carbonic maceration, whole, uncrushed bunches go into a tank filled with carbon dioxide. Without oxygen, enzymes inside each berry start fermenting sugar into alcohol, up to about 2%, and create aromas like banana, bubblegum and kirsch. Then berries burst, and yeast finishes the job. Colour comes out, but little tannin.

steps.title: Semi-carbonic
steps.body: Most Beaujolais uses semi-carbonic maceration. Whole bunches go into the tank; the weight crushes the bottom ones, which ferment normally, producing CO2 that fills the tank. The upper berries undergo carbonic maceration. The result: fruity, soft wines with low tannin. Some crus use traditional crushing for more structure.

steps.prompt: What does carbonic maceration typically produce?
options: Fruity, soft wines with banana or bubblegum notes
steps.explanation: Intracellular fermentation gives fruity aromas and little tannin.

steps.title: Beaujolais Nouveau
steps.body: Beaujolais Nouveau is made fast, by semi-carbonic maceration, and released on the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest. It's light, fruity and meant for immediate drinking. Its fame in the 1980s and 1990s made Beaujolais a household name, but also hurt its reputation for serious wine.

steps.prompt: Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third ____ of November.
steps.explanation: The third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Carbonic maceration ferments whole berries in CO2
It gives fruity, soft wines with banana and bubblegum notes
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November
